content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. Stewed chicken with edible skin stays juicy and flavorful, while providing valuable nutrients such as high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken belongs to the pheasant family and was domesticated more than 8,000 years ago.
Stewing retains more moisture than frying because the meat cooks slowly in liquid.
Chicken skin is rich in collagen, which can benefit skin, hair, and joint health.
Many cultures have signature stewed chicken recipes: French pot‑au‑feu, Indian chicken curry, and Russian chicken stew with vegetables.
Poultry is classified as “white meat,” making it easier to digest compared with red meat.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Stewed chicken provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and vitamin B12, which are essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies selenium, phosphorus, and zinc, nutrients important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low fat (without skin)
items.content: When prepared without added fats, stewed chicken remains a lean source of nutrients.

items.title: Collagen in the skin
items.content: Edible skin adds collagen, which may support skin elasticity and joint health.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken can harbor Salmonella; ensure the internal temperature reaches 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: High sodium in prepared dishes
items.content: Stews made with soy sauce, bouillon, or added salt can be high in sodium.

items.title: Caloric skin
items.content: Chicken skin contains more fat and calories, so those watching weight should consume it in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed chicken can be served as a main course, shredded into salads, added to sandwiches, soups, and pasta dishes. The skin can be eaten together with the meat or removed according to preference. Garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a light sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked stewed chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑size bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings are the meat of a chicken's wing, usually skinless and unseasoned. In this version they are precooked (boiled or baked) and ready to eat after reheating. The wings have a mild flavor, a slight sweetness and a crisp texture when properly heated.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are a staple of American cuisine, famously served as “Buffalo wings”.
In Japan they are often glazed with teriyaki sauce, while in Korea they appear in spicy “yangnyeom” style.
Chicken wings contain more collagen than most other parts of the bird, which can be beneficial for skin and joints.
They have been served as a bar snack since the early 20th century.
The United States celebrates “National Chicken Wing Day” each year, dedicated to this dish.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Wings provide a good source of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: They supply niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Wings contain iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation, immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Makes them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and moderate fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Wings contain more fat than most other chicken cuts; those monitoring fat intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Sodium and preservatives
items.content: Precooked products may contain added salt and preservatives; people with hypertension or kidney issues should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Proper heating
items.content: Insufficiently reheated wings can harbor harmful bacteria; heat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat wings in the microwave, oven, or skillet. Serve them as a snack, in salads, tacos, or with sauces such as barbecue, cheese, or hot sauce. For extra crispness, bake at 200 °C for 10–12 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep precooked wings refrigerated at 0–4 °C for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 2 months. Always reheat thoroughly before eating. Discard if the product develops an off‑odor, discoloration, or a slimy texture.

cream-of-wheat-regular-or-quick-made-wit.title: Cream of Wheat, regular or quick, made with water, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Cream of Wheat is a finely milled wheat farina made from whole wheat kernels. It is sold in regular and quick‑cooking varieties and is typically prepared with water without added fat, making it a low‑calorie breakfast option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cream of Wheat was introduced in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly became popular for its smooth texture.
The quick‑cooking version uses finer particles, reducing cooking time to 1–2 minutes while retaining the same nutrient profile.
Traditionally it is served with sugar, honey, fruit, or nuts, but the basic product contains no added fats.
The wheat used is a good source of iron and B‑vitamins.
In some countries the product is known as wheat porridge or wheat polenta.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Cream of Wheat provides easily absorbable iron that supports normal blood formation.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared with water and no added oil, it contains virtually no fat, suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The fine texture makes it gentle on the stomach, making it a good choice for people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Contains soluble fiber
items.content: Soluble fiber helps regulate blood sugar levels and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Individuals with wheat or gluten intolerance may experience allergic reactions when consuming Cream of Wheat.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The product can cause a rapid rise in blood glucose, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid may reduce the absorption of certain minerals; pairing with vitamin C‑rich foods can mitigate this.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Combine 30 g of cream with 1 cup of water, bring to a boil and cook 1–2 minutes for quick‑cook or 5–7 minutes for regular. Add fruit, berries, honey, nuts, or spices such as cinnamon or vanilla to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, airtight container in a cool place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator to prevent moisture and mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Steamed perch retains most of its nutrients and delicate flavor. It is a lean source of protein, rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as selenium and phosphorus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Steaming preserves up to 95 % of vitamin B12, which is often lost during frying.
Perch belongs to the salmon family and is considered a more environmentally friendly alternative to salmon.
In the wild, perch feeds on small crustaceans, enriching its flesh with trace minerals.
Steamed perch is a traditional dish in Scandinavian cuisine, often served with herbs and lemon.
It cooks quickly: 10‑12 minutes of steaming is enough for full doneness.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support heart health, reduce inflammation, and aid brain function.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Fish protein is easily digestible and helps build and repair muscle tissue.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and B12 are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system maintenance.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and phosphorus
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, while phosphorus is essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Steamed perch is a light option suitable for weight management.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy metal contamination
items.content: Like other fish, perch can contain trace amounts of mercury or cadmium; choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: People with a sensitive stomach may experience discomfort if they consume large portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve steamed perch hot, drizzled with lemon juice or a yogurt‑dill sauce. It pairs well with boiled potatoes, quinoa, or fresh vegetable salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked steamed perch in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: A low‑fat bran with fruit muffin is a baked snack enriched with whole wheat bran and pieces of dried fruit. With a modest fat content (2600 kcal per 100 g) it fits well into diet plans, while the natural fruit sweetness provides flavor without added sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bran is a rich source of dietary fiber that supports regular bowel movements.
Dried fruit retains most of the vitamins and minerals found in fresh fruit.
Low‑fat recipes often replace butter with applesauce or yogurt, lowering calories while keeping moisture.
Muffins are easy to portion into individual packs, making them popular in school cafeterias and office snack boxes.
When stored properly, the muffin stays fresh for up to 5 days.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Bran provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, which aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Reduced fat helps control overall calorie intake, beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from fruit
items.content: Dried fruit adds vitamin C, potassium and iron, supporting immune function and energy metabolism.

items.title: Stable blood‑sugar release
items.content: Complex carbohydrates from bran release glucose slowly, preventing rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Fiber acts as a prebiotic, fostering growth of beneficial intestinal bacteria.

items.title: Wheat/gluten allergy
items.content: Bran contains gluten, so the product is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar from dried fruit
items.content: Although low‑fat, the natural sugars in dried fruit may affect blood‑sugar levels, which diabetics should monitor.

items.title: Excessive fiber intake
items.content: Very high fiber consumption can cause bloating and gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Preservatives in commercial versions
items.content: Some factory‑made muffins may contain additives for longer shelf life; always check the ingredient list.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The muffin can be enjoyed as a quick snack, sliced and paired with low‑fat yogurt, cottage cheese, or nut butter. It also works well crumbled over salads, as a base for dessert parfaits, or simply taken on the go.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the muffin in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer freshness keep it refrigerated – up to 7 days – or freeze individual portions, where it retains quality for about 3 months. Discard if you notice mold or off‑odors.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-and-meat-restaura.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce and Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce and meat is a popular Italian-inspired dish that combines cooked pasta, a velvety cream sauce, and tender pieces of stewed meat (usually beef or pork). The dish is rich in flavor, aroma, and nutrients, making it suitable for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is often made from heavy cream, butter, and Parmesan, giving the dish its characteristic silky taste.
Traditionally in Italy, flat noodles such as fettuccine or tagliatelle are used because they hold the sauce well.
The dish gained wide popularity in the United States in the mid‑20th century when American restaurants adapted Italian recipes to local tastes.
Adding meat makes the meal more filling and boosts its protein content, which is valued in sports nutrition.
The cream sauce can be swapped for a lighter version with yogurt or milk to reduce calories.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium from cream
items.content: The cream sauce supplies calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and pasta are rich in B1, B2, B6, and B12 vitamins, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy density
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from pasta and fats from the sauce offers sustained satiety.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Red meat is a good source of heme iron, helping prevent anemia.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and meat make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑watching individuals.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Cream and butter contain saturated fats, which can raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Salt is often added for flavor; people with hypertension should limit its amount.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: The cream sauce may trigger reactions in those allergic to dairy or unable to digest lactose.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the pasta al dente, then toss it with hot cream sauce and previously sautéed meat. Serve immediately, topped with grated Parmesan and fresh herbs such as parsley or basil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat gently, adding a splash of milk or cream to restore the sauce’s creaminess. Freezing is recommended only for the sauce without pasta.

content.title: About
content.content: A pie shell is a ready‑made or semi‑ready layer of dough designed to form the base of sweet and savory pies. It is typically made from wheat flour, butter or margarine, water and a pinch of salt. Thin, crisp and lightly golden, it provides a convenient foundation for any filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional American “pie crust” is often made with cold butter to create a flaky texture.
European “shortcrust” pies use more butter and result in a denser, tender base.
Gluten‑free versions replace wheat flour with rice, corn or almond flour.
A shell can be blind‑baked (without filling) for tarts, or fully covered when the filling is added on top.
Frozen pre‑made shells speed up preparation while still delivering a crisp finish after baking.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: The crust provides carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with fuel.

items.title: Contains some protein
items.content: Wheat flour contributes a modest amount of plant‑based protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Iron and magnesium
items.content: In small quantities the crust adds minerals that support muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional shells contain wheat, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Shells made with a lot of butter or margarine can be high in calories and saturated fats.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Some ready‑made shells are salty, which should be considered on low‑sodium diets.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Besides gluten, shells may contain dairy if butter is used.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the shell as a base for fruit, berry, custard, meat, vegetable or cheese pies. It can be partially pre‑baked (blind baked) to prevent sogginess, then filled and finished in the oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a fresh shell in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Frozen shells keep for about 3 months; thaw them in the fridge before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Sucralose is an artificial sweetener derived from sugar by replacing three hydroxyl groups with chlorine atoms. The powder contains virtually no calories, is about 600 times sweeter than sugar, and remains stable under heat, making it popular in food manufacturing and home cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sucralose was discovered in 1976 by scientists at Johns Hopkins University.
It is 600–800 times sweeter than sucrose while providing virtually no calories.
Sucralose is heat‑stable, so it can be used in baking, boiling, and frying.
Unlike some sweeteners, it is not fermented in the gastrointestinal tract and does not raise blood glucose levels.
Sucralose is approved by more than 100 regulatory agencies, including the US FDA and the EU EFSA.

items.title: Weight‑management support
items.content: Zero calories allow it to replace sugar, reducing overall energy intake.

items.title: Does not raise blood sugar
items.content: Because it is not metabolized, sucralose does not cause glucose spikes, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Thermal stability
items.content: The sweetener retains its sweetness during baking, cooking, and frying, enabling sugar‑free recipes.

items.title: Non‑cariogenic
items.content: Sucralose does not feed oral bacteria that cause tooth decay.

items.title: Individual intolerance
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience gastrointestinal discomfort at high doses.

items.title: Not recommended for children under 3
items.content: Long‑term safety data for this age group are limited.

items.title: Possible impact on gut microbiota
items.content: Some studies suggest chronic consumption may alter the composition of intestinal bacteria.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Sucralose powder can be added to tea, coffee, sauces, baked goods, desserts, and beverages. Typical dosage is about 1 g (≈1 tsp) per 100 g of product, but follow the manufacturer’s guidelines.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. When kept properly, it remains good for up to 2 years.

content.title: About
content.content: Tamale casserole with meat is a layered baked dish made from corn masa (the dough used for tamales) with savory meat (usually beef or pork), sauce, and sometimes vegetables between the layers. It is baked until a golden crust forms, preserving the traditional flavor of Mexican tamales.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamales are one of the oldest dishes in Mesoamerica, prepared since the Maya and Aztec eras.
The casserole version allows cooking large quantities at once, making it ideal for family meals and celebrations.
Traditional fillings include chili, giving the dish its characteristic heat.
Corn masa is rich in B‑vitamins and dietary fiber.
In some Mexican regions the filling may include black beans or cheese, but the classic version contains only meat.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates from corn masa
items.content: They release energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and corn masa together provide thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Corn masa adds fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: If fatty cuts of meat are used, the dish can be high in saturated fats, which may be a concern for heart‑related conditions.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Salt and sauces added to the filling can increase sodium, important for people with hypertension.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to corn products.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The casserole is fairly calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve the tamale casserole hot, cut into individual portions. It pairs well with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, or fresh herbs. A squeeze of lime adds a bright acidity.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the casserole to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, portion and freeze; reheating in the oven or microwave retains flavor and texture.
